entities.summary:
Guam is an island and organized, unincorporated territory of the United States in the Micronesia subregion of the western Pacific Ocean. With 160,000 people on 549 km², Guam is the southernmost and largest island in the Mariana Islands. Its residents are US citizens, but like Puerto Rico's residents, they cannot vote in presidential elections. Guam hosts major US military installations — Andersen Air Force Base and Naval Station Guam — making it one of the most strategically important US military positions in the western Pacific.

Chamorro people inhabited Guam for at least 3,500 years before Magellan's arrival in 1521 made it the first Pacific island visited by Europeans. Spanish colonization (from 1668) and missionary activity devastated the Chamorro population — estimated at 50,000–100,000 in 1668 and reduced to approximately 5,000 by 1700 through disease, warfare, and forced relocation. Spain transferred Guam to the United States after the Spanish-American War (1898).

Japanese occupation (1941–1944) during World War II was marked by brutality against Chamorro civilians; US liberation in August 1944 was achieved through intense fighting at the Battle of Guam. The Cold War transformed Guam into a major forward base for US power projection in Asia. In the 21st century, US military buildup — transferring Marines from Okinawa — has made Guam central to US military strategy vis-à-vis China and North Korea. The ongoing question of Guam's political status (territory vs. statehood vs. independence) remains unresolved.
